#1
L: For my favor, the supreme secret called adhyātma — the word that was spoken by you — by that this delusion of mine is departed.
I: Out of kindness to me you have spoken the supreme secret teaching called adhyātma; through that teaching this confusion of mine has gone.
N: Chapter 11 opens with Arjuna speaking, thanking Kṛṣṇa for the teaching just given (chapters 2–10). Guhyam adhyātma-saṃjñitam, 'the secret called adhyātma', names that teaching by the technical term Kṛṣṇa himself used for it (adhyātma, 'pertaining to the self', defined at 8.3 as svabhāva, one's own essential nature); it is kept untranslated here as a named term, the way the poem's other technical words are. The sentence has no separate main verb: paramaṃ guhyam adhyātmasaṃjñitam all describe vacaḥ, 'the word', in apposition — 'the word, [namely] the supreme secret called adhyātma, which was spoken by you'. Two sandhis to notice: tat + śakyam-type -t + ś- patterns recur through the chapter (see v.4), and tvayā + uktam fuses to tvayoktam, -ā + u- → -o-, as at mohaḥ + ayam → moho'yam below (-aḥ + a- → -o with the avagraha marking the lost a-).
#2
L: The origin and passing-away indeed of beings have been heard by me in detail, and from you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, your imperishable greatness too.
I: I have already heard from you, in detail, of the birth and passing of all beings, and of your own greatness that never fades, lotus-eyed one.
N: Bhavāpyayau, 'origin-and-dissolution', is a dvandva (pair) compound in the dual, its two members glued together as one idea, the coming-to-be and passing-away of all beings — a theme Kṛṣṇa develops throughout chapters 7–10. Kamalapatrākṣa, 'lotus-petal-eyed', is an epithet of Kṛṣṇa; tvattaḥ, 'from you', is the ablative with the emphatic -tas suffix seen also in mattaḥ 'from me'. The second line's verb is understood by ellipsis: '[I have heard] your imperishable greatness too' repeats śrutau from the first line without restating it, a common economy in Sanskrit.
#3
L: So it is, as you have described yourself, O supreme lord; I wish to see your lordly form, O highest of beings.
I: It is just as you have described yourself, supreme lord — now I want to see that majestic form, highest of beings.
N: Āttha is an irregular perfect ('you have said'), from the defective root ah, which supplies only perfect-tense forms (āha 'he said' appeared throughout chapter 1). Parameśvara and puruṣottama are both vocatives addressed to Kṛṣṇa, 'supreme lord' and 'highest of persons' — titles that anticipate the vision to come. Rūpam aiśvaram, 'the lordly form', uses aiśvara, an adjective from īśvara 'lord', which recurs through the chapter (yogeśvara v.4, mahāyogeśvara v.9, yogam aiśvaram v.8) binding these opening verses together.
#4
L: If you think that it can be seen by me, O lord — then, O lord of yoga, show me your imperishable self.
I: If you think I am able to see it, Lord, then show me your imperishable self, lord of yoga.
N: Yogeśvara, 'lord of yoga', is Arjuna's climactic address, matched in v.9 when Sañjaya calls Kṛṣṇa mahāyogeśvaraḥ, 'the great lord of yoga', as he reveals the form. Tacchakyam is tat + śakyam, -t + ś- → -cch-, a sandhi that recurs at v.1's tatra note; śakyam is a gerundive, 'able to be done', used impersonally with an instrumental agent (mayā draṣṭum śakyam, 'it is possible for it to be seen by me' — i.e. 'I am able to see it'), the same construction returning as a personal passive in v.8's śakyase.
#5
L: Behold, Pārtha, my forms, by the hundreds and by the thousands — of many kinds, divine, of many colors and shapes.
I: Look, Arjuna, at my forms — hundreds of them, thousands of them, of every kind, divine, of every color and shape.
N: The Blessed Lord now answers, granting Arjuna's request. Śataśas and sahasraśas are distributive adverbs built with the suffix -śas, 'by the hundred', 'by the thousand' — the same formation as vistaraśaḥ in v.2. The compounds nānāvidha and nānāvarṇākṛti, 'of many kinds' and 'of many colors and shapes', both use nānā, 'various', which will recur as aneka, 'many, numerous', through the catalogue of verses 10–11.
#6
L: Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts too; behold many wonders never seen before, O Bhārata.
I: Look at the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts as well; behold many marvels never seen before, Bhārata.
N: A roll-call of Vedic deity-classes: the twelve Ādityas (solar gods), the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twin Aśvins, and the storm-god Maruts — the standard thirty-three gods of the older pantheon, now subsumed into Kṛṣṇa's form. The whole string pañyādityānvasūnrudrānaśvinau is one written word only because each accusative ends in a consonant that joins directly to the next; the reading separates the five names. Bhārata, 'descendant of Bharata', here addresses Arjuna (in chapter 1 the same title was for Dhṛtarāṣṭra) — both houses descend from Bharata.
#7
L: Here, united in one place, behold today the whole world, moving and unmoving together, in my body, O Guḍākeśa — and whatever else you wish to see.
I: Here in my body, Arjuna, see today the whole universe gathered into one place, everything that moves and everything that does not — and whatever else you want to see.
N: Sacarācaram, 'with the moving and the unmoving', is a standard Sanskrit pair for 'everything animate and inanimate', built from cara 'moving' and its negation acara. Guḍākeśa, 'thick-haired' or, by another reading, 'conqueror of sleep', is the same epithet of Arjuna used at 1.24. Yaccānyad is a triple sandhi worth tracing: yat + ca → yac ca (-t + c- → -c c-), then ca + anyat → cānyat (a + a → ā), and the final -t of anyat surfaces as -d before the voiced d- of draṣṭum that follows.
#8
L: But you cannot see me with this eye of your own; I give you a divine eye — behold my lordly yoga.
I: But you cannot see me with your own eyes as they are. I will give you a divine eye — now see my majestic power.
N: Śakyase is the personal-passive use of the gerundive śak(ya) with an infinitive: not 'you can be seen' but 'you are able [to see]', the construction already used impersonally at v.4. The divya cakṣus, 'divine eye', that Kṛṣṇa now grants is the device that makes the whole vision possible — Arjuna's ordinary sight cannot bear it. Yogam aiśvaram, 'majestic yoga' or 'the yoga-power of lordship', names what Arjuna is about to see: not a static form but Kṛṣṇa's own divine capacity in action.
#9
L: Having thus spoken, then, O king, Hari, the great lord of yoga, showed to Pārtha his supreme lordly form.
N: Sañjaya resumes the narration, addressing the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra as rājan, 'O king'. Hari, 'the tawny one', is a name of Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu; mahāyogeśvaraḥ, 'the great lord of yoga', answers Arjuna's own address yogeśvara in v.4. Darśayām āsa is a periphrastic perfect, a formation classical Sanskrit uses for certain derived and causative verbs in place of a simple reduplicated perfect.
#10
L: Of many mouths and eyes, of many marvelous aspects, of many divine ornaments, with many divine weapons raised —
I: with countless mouths and eyes, countless wonders to see, countless divine ornaments, and countless divine weapons raised —
N: This verse and the next are a chain of bahuvrīhi compounds — 'possessive' compounds naming the form by what it has, all in the accusative describing rūpam from v.9 — with no finite verb of their own; the sentence is completed only in v.13's apaśyat, 'he saw'. Each pair of compounds is joined by the same word aneka, 'many, numerous', repeated four times across the two verses, mounting the sense of overwhelming multiplicity.
#11
L: wearing divine garlands and robes, anointed with divine fragrance — the god all-wondrous, infinite, facing every way.
I: wearing divine garlands and robes, anointed with heavenly fragrance — a god of every wonder, without end, facing every direction.
N: The chain of compounds from v.10 concludes here on devam, 'the god' — the grammatical head that all of vv.10–11 have been describing. Viśvatomukham, 'facing every way', is a celebrated old epithet (compare the Vedic viśvataścakṣuḥ, 'eyed on every side'), later echoed at 13.13. Sarvāścaryamayam, 'made wholly of wonder', uses the suffix -maya, '(consisting) of, full of' — the same suffix that will form nāmarūpamaya-type compounds elsewhere in Sanskrit philosophical writing.
#12
L: If in the sky the light of a thousand suns should rise up at once, that would be like the splendor of that great-souled one.
I: If a thousand suns were to blaze up together in the sky, their light would still be no more than a match for the splendor of that great being.
N: One of the poem's most quoted images. Bhavet and syāt are both optative, 'were to be' / 'would be', framing a contrary-to-fact comparison: 'if X were to happen, Y would be [merely] like it'. Mahātman, 'great-souled', a standard honorific compound (mahā + ātman), here names the being whose splendor exceeds even that thousand-sun light — Kṛṣṇa in his cosmic form. Note the run of sandhi: bhavet + yugapat → bhaved yugapat (-t + y- → -d y-), yugapat + utthitā → yugapad utthitā (-t + u- → -d u-), syāt + bhāsaḥ → syād bhāsaḥ (-t + bh- → -d bh-), bhāsaḥ + tasya → bhāsas tasya (-aḥ + t- → -as t-).
#13
L: There, united in one, the whole world divided in many ways, the Pāṇḍava then saw, in the body of the god of gods.
I: There, in the body of the god of gods, Arjuna then saw the whole universe gathered into one, divided in countless ways.
N: This verse finally supplies the finite verb, apaśyat, 'he saw', that the long descriptive sentence of vv.9–11 has been waiting for: what Kṛṣṇa showed, Arjuna now sees. Deva-deva, 'the god of gods', is the poem's title for Kṛṣṇa's cosmic form. Eka-stham ... anekadhā, 'united in one ... divided in many ways', sets side by side the paradox at the heart of the vision — the whole universe is at once one thing and countless things.
#14
L: Then he, overcome with astonishment, his hair bristling, Dhanañjaya — having bowed his head to the god, with hands folded, spoke.
I: Then Arjuna, overwhelmed with wonder, his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the god and, hands folded, began to speak.
N: Vismayāviṣṭaḥ, 'entered by astonishment', uses ā-viś, 'to enter, possess', the same verb that described Arjuna being overcome by pity at 1.28 (kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ); hṛṣṭaromā, 'hair bristling', echoes the shock-symptoms of 1.29 (romaharṣa, 'hair-thrill'), though there from dread and here from awe. Añjali, the cupped-hands gesture of reverence, marks the shift from Sañjaya's narration into the hymn of praise (the Viśvarūpa-stuti) that follows in the verses beyond this chunk. Dhanaṃjaya, 'winner of wealth', Arjuna's title, is spelled here with anusvāra for the class nasal — an orthographic variant, not a real one, and needs no correction note.
